title: Effective field theories of nonlinear fluctuating hydrodynamics in one dimension
abstract: Describing emergent macroscopic phenomena in low spatial dimensions is known to be notoriously challenging, primarily due to strong interactions that render perturbative approaches inapplicable. On the other hand, low-dimensional systems host a wealth of unorthodox phenomena. A prominent example is the emergence of superdiffusive transport in one-dimensional interacting systems, traditionally studied in the framework of nonlinear fluctuating hydrodynamics. After identifying and discussing internal inconsistencies in the previous formulations, in this work we develop a general and systematic approach for constructing effective field theories of one-dimensional hydrodynamic systems in the form of coupled stochastic Langevin-type equations compatible with the physical requirements of local equilibrium states such as the thermodynamic Maxwell relation and fluctuation-dissipation symmetry. We implemented a general numerical integration scheme and exemplified our construction on a simple model of two interacting hydrodynamic modes with a non-Gaussian stationary equilibrium measure.
summary: This paper develops a systematic effective field theory framework for nonlinear fluctuating hydrodynamics in 1D systems. It overcomes limitations of previous models by enforcing key thermodynamic symmetries like the Maxwell relation through a master potential. The work successfully predicts superdiffusive transport regimes and provides robust numerical methods for non-Gaussian equilibrium states.
main_problem: Developing a general and systematic effective field theory approach for nonlinear fluctuating hydrodynamics in one dimension that rigorously respects fundamental symmetry constraints of local equilibrium states.
main_result: The authors successfully construct EFTs by introducing a master potential that manifestly enforces the Maxwell relation, demonstrating superdiffusive transport ($z=3/2$) alongside diffusive modes in a minimal non-Gaussian model.
method: The work combines theoretical construction based on symmetry principles (Maxwell relation) with numerical simulations of stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) and advanced sampling techniques like tilted ensembles.
model_or_system: The study focuses on one-dimensional interacting systems exhibiting emergent phenomena, modeled via nonlinear fluctuating hydrodynamics described by coupled stochastic Langevin-type equations. The analysis is tested on a minimal model featuring two interacting hydrodynamic modes with a non-Gaussian stationary equilibrium measure.
key_observables: Superdiffusive algebraic exponents ($z$), static covariance matrices ($C_{ab}$), and the preservation of symmetry relations like $B_{a|b} = B_{b|a}$.
important_parameters: The dimensionality (one dimension) and the nature of the equilibrium measure (non-Gaussian vs. Gaussian).
main_assumptions: Previous NLFHD formulations are shown to have conceptual issues when applied to non-Gaussian measures, necessitating a symmetry-preserving EFT construction.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate structure factors showing superdiffusive and diffusive broadening over time; other figures compare numerical sampling methods (Metropolis vs. exact) for minimal models.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying limitations in existing NLFHD/MCE approaches to developing a symmetry-enforcing EFT via a master potential, followed by applying this framework to analyze transport properties and test the numerical stability of the resulting SPDEs.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous theoretical tools for describing non-equilibrium dynamics in low dimensions where simple perturbative methods fail, connecting macroscopic hydrodynamics directly to fundamental thermodynamic symmetries.

FIG. 2. Decay of diagonal structure factors and run- ning exponents. The decay of the peaks of diagonal struc- ture factors Sa(vat, t) in the minimal model. The dashed lines show the expected asymptotic decay rates t−1/z for z ∈{3/2, 2}. In the inset we show time-resolved dynami- cal exponents za(t) = −[dlog Sa(vat, t)/d logt]−1 which shows that mode 1 is superdiffusive with limt→∞z1(t) ≈3/2, while mode 2 clearly converges to the expected value z2 = 2. FIG. 3. Stationarity of a Gaussian equilibrium state Peq under dynamics in the cyclic test model. The left panel shows evolution of C (2) which preserves contact form, while the right panel shows the dynamics of equal-time correlators M(n)(t) which evidently fluctuate around expected equilibrium values that are denoted by dashed lines (determined analytically). Simulation parameters: ∆t = 0.04, number of samples 1000, N = 128.

FIG. 4. Dynamical generation of nonzero cumulants M(n>2) under dynamics with a non-cyclic Hessian. The equal-time correlators M(n)(t) are evaluated in equilibrium with an increasing number of samples. The Gaussian prediction limt→∞Mab = δab and limt→∞M(n>2) = 0 are broken. Simulation parameters: ∆t = 0.04, N = 128.

FIG. 5. Stability of the cyclic (left panel) and the consistent (right panel) numerical schemes. The panels show maxx ψ1(x, t) averaged over 100 initial conditions as a function of time for increasing ∆t. The legend denotes the used timestep ∆t and the fraction of trajectories that exhibited instability maxx ψ1(x, t) > 106. The consistent scheme stabilizes the dynamics to a large degree. Parameters: N = 128, c = 0.3, κ = 2, number of samples 100.
